Evals and what they actually measure

How do we know whether a change made the product better, rather than merely different?

1. A Wednesday in Bengaluru

On the morning of 4 February 2026, Meera Rajagopalan, Vice-President of Product at Vipanan Commerce Cloud, had a decision on her desk that her engineering director believed was already made. Vipanan sells a seller-operations console to roughly 14,000 small and mid-sized Indian brands that list on Amazon, Flipkart, Meesho and their own ONDC storefronts. Inside that console sits Vipanan Assist, a text assistant that answers the questions sellers actually ask at eleven at night: why a Meesho return was marked customer-damaged, what the GST-inclusive landed price should be if a courier surcharge changes, how to word a reply to a buyer who has threatened a one-star review.

Assist handles about 260,000 conversations a month. It costs Vipanan around ₹31 lakh a month to run. Three weeks earlier, the model vendor had released a newer, cheaper model. On the vendor's published test suites it scored several points higher than the model Vipanan currently used, and it was faster: median first-token latency fell from 2.4 seconds to 1.1 seconds in Vipanan's own load tests, and the cost per conversation fell from ₹0.42 to ₹0.19. That is a saving of about ₹14 lakh a month, or ₹1.7 crore a year, on a product line whose gross margin the board had asked her to defend.

Rohit Bhandari, the engineering director in Bengaluru, had circulated a one-page note titled Model upgrade: no-brainer. Aparna Sekhri, who ran customer success out of Singapore for the Southeast Asian and Gulf accounts, had replied within the hour: Before we swap anything, can somebody tell me how it handles Hinglish returns queries? That is most of my volume. The exchange, Meera realised, was not a disagreement about the model. It was a disagreement about what had been measured, and about what the measurement entitled anyone to conclude.

2. The idea, stated precisely

An eval — short for evaluation, and used in the singular as a countable noun, "an eval" — is a repeatable measurement of a system's behaviour on a fixed set of inputs, scored against a criterion stated in advance. Each of those five clauses is doing work. Repeatable means you can run it again next month and the comparison is meaningful. System means the whole assembly the user actually touches. Fixed set of inputs means the questions do not change between the two things you are comparing. Scored means something or someone assigns a verdict. Criterion stated in advance means you decided what counted as good before you saw which candidate won.

The practice is older than the current wave of language models. Information-retrieval researchers formalised it at the Text REtrieval Conference, TREC, from 1992: a fixed document collection, a fixed set of queries, human relevance judgements, and a leaderboard. Machine learning inherited the habit through MNIST and then ImageNet from 2009, where a frozen labelled test set became the shared referee for a decade of computer vision. Language modelling picked it up with GLUE in 2018 and, when GLUE saturated, SuperGLUE and then broader suites such as Stanford's HELM in 2022. The problem all of these were invented to solve is simple and permanent: research teams could always show you an example where their system did something impressive, and examples prove nothing about a probabilistic function.

That last phrase is the bridge to the harder point. A large language model is a probabilistic next-token predictor; ask it the same question twice and you may get two different answers. A single impressive transcript is therefore not evidence, it is a sample of size one from a distribution nobody has characterised. An eval exists to turn anecdote into an estimate.

The sentence Meera could repeat in a board meeting without sounding glib: "A benchmark tells us how a model performs on somebody else's test. An eval tells us how our system performs on our task. The vendor gave us the first; we have not yet built the second."

3. How an eval is actually built

Practitioners describe eval-building as six steps, and then, in practice, skip two of them. It is worth walking all six with Vipanan's problem in hand.

Fix the unit of measurement. Meera's unit is one seller conversation passing through the full Assist pipeline — retrieval, prompt assembly, model, tool calls, filter — not one model completion. If she measures the model in isolation she learns something true and irrelevant.

Fix the inputs. Her team sampled 200 real conversations from December and January, stratified so the mix matched production: returns disputes, pricing questions, buyer-reply drafting, account and payout queries. The set is frozen, versioned as assist-core-v3, and stored with the retrieved documents that were live at the time, so that a change in the policy corpus does not silently change the test.

State the criterion. This is where most teams become vague. Vipanan's criterion, written before any candidate was run, has three parts: the answer must be factually consistent with the marketplace policy document retrieved; it must not invent a policy clause, a fee or a deadline; and it must be actionable, meaning a seller could execute it without a follow-up question. All three must hold for the item to pass. A single binary per item makes the arithmetic honest.

Choose the grader. Options are human review, a program that checks a deterministic property, or another model prompted to judge. Vipanan used two operations analysts in Pune grading blind — they did not know which system produced which answer — with a third analyst breaking ties. On a 40-item pilot the two agreed on 34, which is an 85 per cent raw agreement rate. That number matters: the grader's own error sets a ceiling on how small a difference the eval can detect.

Decide the sampling. Because the model is probabilistic, one run per item under-reports variance. Vipanan ran each item three times at the production temperature and scored an item as passing only if it passed all three — a strict rule that captures the seller's actual exposure to a bad night.

Decide the decision rule in advance. Meera wrote it down before the run: ship if the paired improvement is positive and statistically distinguishable from zero, and if no named segment regresses by more than two points. Writing the rule first is what converts a measurement into a decision procedure rather than a source of after-the-fact justification.

4. The arithmetic, done twice

The run finished on 6 February. On the 200-item frozen set, the incumbent model passed 144 items and the new model passed 157. That is 72.0 per cent against 78.5 per cent, an improvement of 6.5 percentage points. Rohit's note rounded this to "seven points better and half the cost".

Treat the two numbers as independent samples, which is how most teams instinctively read them, and the picture is weaker. The standard error of a proportion is the square root of p(1−p)/n. For the incumbent that is the square root of (0.72 × 0.28)/200 = 0.001008, or 0.0318 — about 3.2 points. For the challenger it is the square root of (0.785 × 0.215)/200 = 0.000844, or 0.0291, about 2.9 points. The standard error of the difference is the square root of the sum of the squares: the square root of 0.001008 + 0.000844 = 0.001852, which is 0.0430, or 4.3 points. The observed gap of 6.5 points is therefore 1.51 standard errors — short of the roughly 1.96 conventionally required for 95 per cent confidence. On this reading, Aparna's scepticism is arithmetically justified.

But the two systems answered the same 200 questions, and that pairing is information the independent-samples calculation throws away. The right view is the contingency of agreements and disagreements.

Only 25 of the 200 items discriminate between the systems at all: 19 that the challenger fixes and 6 that it breaks. McNemar's test looks only at those. The statistic is the difference between the discordant cells divided by the square root of their sum: (19 − 6) divided by the square root of 25, which is 13 divided by 5, or 2.60. That comfortably exceeds 1.96. The improvement is real; the earlier calculation was simply asking a less precise question. Note also the six regressions. Six items out of 200 that used to work and now do not is a fact no aggregate score reports.

The second pass. Meera then changed one input: instead of scoring the set as a whole, she split it by language. Of the 200 items, 120 were in English and 80 in Hindi — Devanagari or Romanised. On the English subset the incumbent passed 90 of 120, or 75.0 per cent, and the challenger 103 of 120, or 85.8 per cent, a gain of 10.8 points. On the Hindi subset both passed 54 of 80, or 67.5 per cent. Every point of improvement lived in English.

That would be tolerable if the eval set matched production. It did not. The frozen set was 40 per cent Hindi; Vipanan's February traffic was 63 per cent Hindi or Hinglish, because the seller base had grown fastest in Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh. Re-weighting the segment scores to the production mix gives an expected challenger pass rate of (0.37 × 85.8) + (0.63 × 67.5) = 31.7 + 42.5 = 74.2 per cent, against an incumbent of (0.37 × 75.0) + (0.63 × 67.5) = 27.8 + 42.5 = 70.3 per cent. The honest expected gain is 3.9 points, not 6.5. Same data, same systems, one changed assumption about what the population is.

5. Nuances a learner must acquire

An eval measures a system, a benchmark measures a component

This is the distinction the word "eval" most often hides, because vendors, researchers and product teams all use it. When a model card reports a benchmark score it is measuring weights and a decoding strategy against public questions with public answers. When Meera measures Assist she is measuring retrieval quality, prompt design, tool reliability, the filter and the model together. A change that improves the component can degrade the system: a model that follows instructions more literally may stop making the loose inferences the prompt was quietly relying on.

The criterion is a product decision, not a technical one

"Correct" is not a property that exists independently of what the seller needed. Vipanan's criterion includes actionability precisely because an answer that is true but requires a follow-up question costs the seller a night. Two competent teams can build defensible evals on the same product and reach opposite verdicts because they encoded different views of the job to be done. Argue about the criterion first; the numbers are downstream of it.

Aggregates conceal reversals

The Hindi split is the general case, not a quirk. Whenever a population has segments with different difficulty and different volumes, an average can improve while the segment carrying most of the volume gets worse. The discipline is to name the segments you care about before the run — language, account size, query type, geography — and require that none of them regress. This also protects against the political failure in which the aggregate is reported upward and the regression is discovered by a customer.

One run is not a measurement

Because generation is sampled, the same input can pass on Tuesday and fail on Thursday. Running each item three times, as Vipanan did, converts a point observation into a crude distribution. Teams that run once and see a two-point difference are usually observing sampling noise. Teams that set temperature to zero to make runs reproducible are measuring a system they do not ship, unless they also ship at temperature zero.

Evals decay, and the good ones decay fastest

A frozen set is only representative of the moment it was frozen. Vipanan's set was six months stale on the dimension that mattered most. Worse, once a team optimises against a fixed set, the set stops measuring general quality and starts measuring fit to itself — the familiar Goodhart problem, that a measure adopted as a target ceases to be a good measure. Mature teams hold a second set in reserve that engineers never see, and re-sample the main set on a schedule.

The grader has error too

Vipanan's two analysts agreed on 34 of 40 items. If human graders disagree 15 per cent of the time, an eval cannot reliably resolve differences much smaller than that disagreement. The same applies with more force when another model is used as the judge, which is the cheap and increasingly common option: an LLM judge must itself be validated against human labels before its verdicts are treated as data, and it tends to have systematic biases — toward longer answers, toward its own family of models, toward confident phrasing.

What an eval cannot tell you, however well built

It cannot tell you whether the task is worth doing. It cannot tell you whether sellers would prefer a different product. It is poor at rare catastrophic events: a failure occurring in one conversation in 5,000 will appear zero or one time in a 200-item set, and the difference between zero and one is not information. And it cannot price a regression — the six broken items in Table 1 might be trivial or might each represent a ₹40,000 dispute.

Questions a newcomer should ask before trusting one

Who wrote the criterion, and when relative to the run? What is in the set and does it match this quarter's traffic? How many runs per item? Who or what graded, and how good is the grader? What is the decision rule, and was it fixed in advance? Which segments were checked for regression? Those six questions separate a measurement from a marketing exercise, and none of them require technical training to ask.

6. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the criterion is usually preference rather than correctness, and volume is large enough that a live A/B test on a behavioural metric — retention, task completion, session depth — is often more informative than an offline eval. The offline eval's job there is narrower: catching safety and quality regressions before exposing users, and screening the many candidates down to the two worth testing live.

In B2B products such as Vipanan's, volume per customer is small, the buyer is not the user, and one badly wrong answer to a large account can cost a renewal worth ₹60 lakh. Offline evals matter more because you cannot A/B test your way to confidence on 40 enterprise accounts, and because customers increasingly ask to see the eval in a procurement review. In marketplaces, the difficult wrinkle is that the two sides have different criteria for the same output — a return-policy answer that satisfies a seller may under-serve a buyer — so a single pass rate quietly averages two conflicting objectives, and the honest design has two evals.

Stage changes economics rather than principle. An eight-person startup can afford 60 hand-graded items reviewed by the founders, refreshed monthly, and should not pretend to more rigour than that; the founders' direct grading is a genuine advantage, because criterion and judgement sit in the same head. A large company can afford 2,000-item sets, standing grader panels and continuous regression runs, but pays in latency and politics: the set becomes an asset someone owns, refreshing it becomes a project, and the criterion drifts away from any specific user.

7. Common mistakes, and the cheapest diagnostic for each

Reading a benchmark as an eval. The symptom from outside is a shipping decision justified by a vendor's published number or a leaderboard position. The underlying misunderstanding is that the model is the product. The cheapest diagnostic is one question in the review: "Show me ten inputs from that test set." If nobody can, the test measured somebody else's task.

Choosing the criterion after seeing the results. The symptom is a metric that changes between the first review and the second, always in the direction that supports the preferred conclusion. The misunderstanding is that an eval is a description rather than a decision rule. The diagnostic is to ask for the dated document in which the criterion and the shipping threshold were written down, and to notice whether one exists.

Reporting the aggregate only. The symptom is a single headline number in the deck with no segment table behind it. The misunderstanding is that the population is homogeneous. The diagnostic is to ask for the paired contingency table: how many items got better, how many got worse. A team that cannot produce the "got worse" count has not looked.

Treating a small difference as a result. The symptom is a decision made on a two-point move in a 100-item set. The misunderstanding is that a percentage computed from a sample is the truth rather than an estimate. The diagnostic is to ask how many items actually changed verdict; if the answer is four, the finding is noise wearing a percentage sign.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Meera's February would have looked like this. In October, when the seller mix began shifting north, the eval set would have been re-stratified, with language, query type and account tier named as protected segments. The criterion — policy-consistent, non-inventive, actionable — would have been in a versioned document with the shipping rule attached: positive paired improvement, no protected segment down more than two points. The run would have produced a contingency table rather than a headline, and the nineteen fixes and six regressions would each have been read by a human. Aparna in Singapore would have received the Hindi and Gulf-account slices as a matter of routine rather than having to ask. And the whole exercise would have cost about four analyst-days — roughly ₹90,000 — against a decision worth ₹1.7 crore a year, which is the ratio that makes evals an easy purchase and their absence hard to defend.

9. What Meera decided

She did not ship the swap, and she did not reject it. She approved a staged rollout to the English-preferring segment, about 37 per cent of conversations, capturing roughly ₹5 lakh a month of the saving, while the team built a 150-item Hindi and Hinglish set with graders in Lucknow and Jaipur who actually sold on Meesho. The reasoning she gave the board was narrow and defensible: the paired evidence shows the challenger is genuinely better where it was tested well, and shows nothing at all about where most of the volume is. Buying ₹5 lakh a month of certain saving while spending three weeks to earn the right to the other ₹9 lakh struck her as better than either shipping on a benchmark or refusing on a hunch.

What to learn next follows directly. Golden sets and LLM-as-judge is the natural sequel, because Vipanan cannot afford human graders at the scale the Hindi set implies; understanding how a judge model is validated is what makes cheap grading trustworthy. Benchmarks, leaderboards and what SOTA means sharpens the distinction this page rests on. Drift and silent regression matters because the interesting failure is not the one you catch during an upgrade but the one that arrives in July when the vendor updates a model behind an unchanged version string.

Two questions to sit with.

1. Vipanan's criterion had three clauses and produced one binary per item. What is gained and what is lost by collapsing three judgements into one, and under what circumstances would you insist on scoring the three separately even though it makes the arithmetic messier?

2. Suppose the six regressions in Table 1 all occurred on payout queries from the twelve largest accounts. Nothing in the aggregate changes. What should change in the decision, and what does that imply about the assumption that every item in an eval set is worth the same?

Prameya Health Cloud: The Instrument and the Deadline

Every number the company is contractually required to report has improved. The one number nobody agreed to report has not.

1. Sunday night, 15 November 2026

Dr Ira Bhattacharya had been Chief Product Officer of Prameya Health Cloud for nineteen months, and an internal-medicine registrar for six years before that. At a quarter past eleven on a Sunday night in Jubilee Hills, with the steering committee due at nine the next morning and the board on 4 December, she had three documents open on the same screen and could not make them agree.

The first was the quarterly compliance audit from Sushrut Hospitals Group: 97.1 per cent, the best figure Prameya had ever recorded against the accuracy service level in its master agreement. The second was a shadow evaluation her Toronto data scientist had run three weeks earlier, which said the model Prameya was being forced to migrate to was worse on two of six clinical criteria, one of them the omission of documented negative findings. The third was a two-page minute from the quality committee of Nandanvan Healthcare's Pune unit, dated 28 October, recording a near-miss: a discharge summary generated by Prameya Scribe had failed to carry forward a recorded drug-sensitivity note from the admission record. A ward pharmacist had caught it before dispensing. No patient had been harmed. The committee had asked, politely and in writing, how Prameya's accuracy figure of 97.1 per cent was compatible with what had happened.

Ira had drafted three answers to that question and deleted all three.

2. How Prameya got here

Prameya Health Cloud was founded in Hyderabad in 2020 by Kartik Rao, a former enterprise-software executive, and Dr Meenakshi Iyer, a Chennai physician who had spent four years trying to make electronic medical records usable in a busy outpatient department. Their product, Prameya Scribe, listens to a consultation or takes dictation, and produces a structured clinical note, a discharge summary and a suggested procedure code. The pitch was never that it replaced the doctor. It was that a consultant seeing sixty outpatients in a session could stop typing and start looking at the patient, and that documentation quality would rise rather than fall because the machine never got tired at four in the afternoon.

The Indian market made the pitch land. The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission had pushed hospitals toward structured, portable records; NABH accreditation cycles created recurring documentation audits; and the large listed chains had already invested heavily in digital infrastructure, which meant integration was possible rather than aspirational. By November 2026 Prameya served fourteen hospital groups across India, generated about 4.2 lakh notes a month, and had annual recurring revenue of ₹58 crore. It also had one substantial international customer: Al Yasmin Medical Group, a Dubai operator of twenty-three clinics, contributing ₹4.2 crore a year on a contract due for renewal on 15 January 2027.

The decision that constrains everything. In September 2022, competing against Upchaar Systems for the Sushrut account — at the time a company-making deal — Prameya agreed to a contractual accuracy service level. Annexure C of the master agreement defines it precisely: each quarter, the hospital's medical records department selects 200 notes; a physician appointed by the hospital marks each note acceptable or not acceptable as a whole; Prameya must achieve 95 per cent or better; three consecutive failures trigger a price renegotiation clause that runs in the hospital's favour. Annexure C also excludes intensive-care notes and any case flagged as clinically complex from the sample, on the reasonable-sounding grounds of physician reviewer time.

Meenakshi negotiated and signed that annexure. It has been copied, more or less verbatim, into eleven of Prameya's fourteen Indian contracts and into the Al Yasmin agreement. It is the only definition of quality that any customer has agreed to, the only one that appears in a sales deck, and the only one that Prameya's own dashboards are built around.

3. The industry around it

Clinical documentation software in India sits between three pressures. Hospitals want throughput and accreditation evidence. Doctors want their time back and are, correctly, sceptical of software that adds clicks. Regulation is tightening: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act constrains what patient data may be retained, and for what stated purpose, which bears directly on whether Prameya may keep a library of real notes to test against — the consent language in nine of its fourteen contracts covers "service provision and quality assurance" and is silent on model development.

Competitively, Upchaar Systems is the closest rival and has been more aggressive on price; several global ambient-documentation vendors are entering India through hospital-chain partnerships; and the general-purpose model vendors keep making the underlying capability cheaper, which is good for Prameya's margin and bad for its defensibility. Prameya's answer to the defensibility question, in every investor conversation, has been its clinical evaluation capability — the claim that it knows how to measure whether a note is safe, and that a general-purpose vendor does not.

The forcing event. On 6 August 2026, Prameya's model vendor announced that the model version Prameya had pinned since early 2025 would be withdrawn on 31 December 2026. Continued access on dedicated capacity is available at roughly 2.4 times the current unit price. Prameya's inference bill is currently ₹41 lakh a month.

4. The situation in detail

The timeline matters, and so does what was believed at each point.

June 2026. Lena Hofmann's redesign of the review screen shipped. The old screen showed the generated note in a plain edit box; the new one shows a clean, formatted document with a single prominent Approve button and edits available behind a pencil icon. Doctor satisfaction scores rose sharply. Mean review time per note fell from 74 seconds to 41. This was reported to the board in July as an efficiency win, and it was received as one.

6 August. Deprecation notice. Sandeep Kulkarni's engineering team in Pune began migration work the following week.

September. Prameya rolled out a new in-product incident form, making it markedly easier for a hospital user to flag a problematic note; previously incidents came through account managers. Reported near-misses rose in September and again in October.

Late September. Rhea Fernandes in Toronto, who had joined in February and had been asking for six months to build a proper evaluation set, was finally given three weeks. She assembled 480 de-identified notes stratified across specialty, note type and language of dictation, and wrote a six-clause criterion before running anything: factual consistency with the source encounter; completeness of active medications with doses; carry-forward of documented allergies and sensitivities; preservation of documented negative findings; absence of invented findings; and coding-suggestion validity. She graded with a judge model calibrated against two physicians on a 90-note subset.

17 October. Rhea's results circulated. The candidate model was better on four clauses and worse on two: carry-forward of documented allergies, and preservation of documented negatives.

28 October. The Nandanvan near-miss.

4 November. Ira asked for a retrospective count. Prameya's engineering team searched three months of notes for the specific pattern — a documented sensitivity present in the admission record and absent from the discharge summary — and found eleven instances across roughly 12.6 lakh notes. That is about one in 115,000. Nine of the eleven had been caught downstream by a pharmacist or a nurse.

11 November. In a routine capacity review, Ira learned something she had not been told: since 9 October, roughly 40 per cent of production traffic had been served by the candidate model. Sandeep's team had begun a staged migration for latency and stability testing, believing quite reasonably that the model change was a technical substitution already approved in the August deprecation plan. Nobody had connected this to the near-miss on 28 October. Nobody, as of Sunday night, could say with confidence which model had produced the Nandanvan summary, because the routing logs retain the model identifier for only thirty days.

5. The people

Dr Ira Bhattacharya, Chief Product Officer, Hyderabad. Position: the company cannot certify a migration it has not measured against the failure mode that actually occurred. What she is not saying: she approved the June review-screen redesign enthusiastically and has begun to suspect it is the largest contributor to whatever has changed.

Kartik Rao, co-founder and CEO, Hyderabad and Mumbai. Position: complete the migration on schedule, protect the margin, keep the 97.1 per cent in the deck. What he is not saying: a Series C term sheet under discussion is conditioned on gross-margin improvement and on the Al Yasmin renewal closing, and the ₹41 lakh monthly inference line is the largest single lever he has.

Dr Meenakshi Iyer, co-founder and Chief Medical Officer, Chennai. Position: halt the migration entirely until a clinical safety evaluation exists, and tell Nandanvan's quality committee everything. What she is not saying: she wrote and signed Annexure C, including the exclusion of intensive-care and complex cases, and knows that the audit's design is part of why the near-miss pattern was invisible for three months.

Sandeep Kulkarni, VP Engineering, Pune. Position: 31 December is a hard external date; the migration is 40 per cent done and the remaining work is six weeks; a pause costs more than it saves. What he is not saying: he did not escalate the October traffic shift because he classified it as infrastructure, and he is aware that the thirty-day log retention he specified last year now makes the Nandanvan attribution unrecoverable.

Rhea Fernandes, Senior Data Scientist, Toronto. Position: the shadow evaluation is the only measurement Prameya has of the thing that matters, and it says the candidate is worse on exactly the clause implicated in the near-miss. What she is not saying: her judge model comes from the same vendor family as the system being graded, her physician calibration produced a kappa of 0.58, and her set of 480 notes gives her almost no power to detect an event occurring once in 115,000.

Lena Hofmann, Design Director, Berlin. Position: the model is a distraction; the review screen has removed friction from a step that exists precisely to create friction, and she wants mandatory field-level confirmation for allergies and medication doses. What she is not saying: reintroducing friction would reverse the efficiency metric she was promoted on in July, and her Berlin team's roadmap for the first quarter has nothing else in it.

Faisal Rahman, Director of Customer Success, Singapore, covering the Gulf. Position: nothing about the system serving Al Yasmin should change before 15 January. What he is not saying: Al Yasmin's clinical operations lead has been running a quiet three-clinic pilot with Upchaar Systems since September, and Faisal has known for five weeks.

Gaurav Nanda, VP Sales, New Jersey. Position: the accuracy number is the single most effective element of the pitch and must not move. What he is not saying: he quoted 97.1 per cent, without the Annexure C sampling caveat, in a proposal to a United States telehealth group that goes to their clinical governance committee in February.

7. Voices

The two clauses it loses on are rare and severe. Averaging a common mild gain against a rare severe loss and calling the result 'better' is not a measurement, it is an accounting choice."

Rhea Fernandes, reply-all, 14 November, 02.10 IST

"Ira, I want to be careful here. I signed Annexure C. In 2022 it was the most rigorous thing anyone in this market was offering. It is now the reason we cannot see our own problem. I will say that in the room if you want me to."

Lena Hofmann, design review, 10 November

"Al Yasmin's clinical lead asked me on Thursday whether our accuracy figure includes complex cases. I said I would come back to her. Please tell me what to say."

Faisal Rahman, email to Ira and Kartik, 14 November

8. The options as Ira currently sees them

Option A: complete the migration by 31 December as planned. The candidate model is better on the contracted measure and on four of six clinical clauses; it saves ₹18 lakh a month; and the alternative is a ₹98 lakh monthly bill on a model that will eventually go anyway. Add monitoring in the first quarter. The objection is that Prameya would be certifying a change on an instrument that, by Exhibit 2's own footnote, cannot see the failure that has already occurred once in production.

Option B: pause the migration, buy dedicated legacy capacity for three months, and build a 2,000-note physician-graded set first. This costs about ₹1.71 crore in additional inference plus ₹27 lakh for the set, and it consumes the quarter. It also produces the artefact that Prameya's investor story claims already exists. The objection is that ninety days of delay does not obviously produce a safer answer — the event rate is one in 115,000, and a 2,000-note set has essentially no power to detect it either.

Option C: migrate, but reintroduce friction in the review screen for allergy and medication fields. Fourteen lakh rupees and five weeks; adds eighteen seconds per note, reversing most of the efficiency gain that customers have been enjoying since July. The objection is that Prameya has no evidence that field-level confirmation changes doctor behaviour rather than producing a second reflexive click, and that it would be shipping a hypothesis as a safety control.

Ira has written all three on a page. She has also written, underneath them, a sentence she has not shown anyone: all three assume the question is which model to run. Exhibit 4 suggests the largest single change in the system this year was made by a designer, not a model vendor. Exhibit 3 suggests she cannot tell whether the world got worse or the reporting got better. Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 disagree about the direction of the change because they encode different judgements about how to weigh a rare severe error against a common mild one — and the judgement in Exhibit 1 was made by Meenakshi in a negotiation in 2022, under commercial pressure, and has never been revisited. Prameya has been running for four years on a definition of quality it accepted rather than chose.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The steering committee meets at nine on Monday 16 November. The board meets on 4 December and will be shown the quarter's accuracy figure and the margin plan. The incumbent model disappears on 31 December; dedicated capacity requires a three-month commitment signed by 1 December. Nandanvan's quality committee has asked for a written response by 30 November, and Nandanvan's NABH accreditation visit is in February. Al Yasmin decides on 15 January, and Faisal needs an answer to a direct question this week. Seven of eleven Indian contracts allow a pricing renegotiation if Annexure C is reopened. Nine of fourteen consent clauses cover quality assurance and are silent on model development, which constrains what Rhea may legally add to an evaluation set. The Pune engineering team has six weeks of committed migration work and no slack. Prameya has ₹38 crore of cash and is raising.

10. Questions for discussion

1. What, precisely, does the Annexure C figure of 97.1 per cent measure? Name the population it samples, the criterion it applies and the party that controls each.

2. Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 point in opposite directions on the same migration. Identify every substantive difference between the two instruments, and say which differences could be removed and which are irreducible.

3. Exhibit 3 shows near-misses more than quadrupling. What would you need to know before treating that as evidence of anything, and what could Prameya do this week to find out?

4. Exhibit 4's falling edit rate is reported internally as an improvement. Construct the strongest case that it is an improvement and the strongest case that it is the most alarming number in the case. What single measurement would separate them?

5. Suppose Ira builds the perfect evaluation set. Given an event rate of roughly one in 115,000, what could such a set actually establish about the safety of the candidate model, and what would have to be measured some other way? What does your answer imply about how much of Prameya's assurance should come from offline evaluation at all?

6. What should Ira do on Monday morning — in the steering committee, in the written response to Nandanvan due on 30 November, and at the board on 4 December? What exactly would she say about the 97.1 per cent, and what would she be committing the company to by saying it?

11. Sunday night, continued

At ten past one Ira closed the shadow-evaluation spreadsheet and opened the Nandanvan minute again. The committee's question was one sentence long and entirely fair: how is an accuracy figure of 97.1 per cent compatible with the omission described above?

She could answer that the two things measure different populations, which was true and would sound like an evasion. She could answer that the near-miss was one event in 115,000, which was true and would sound worse. She could answer that Prameya had discovered the pattern itself and was strengthening its controls, which was true, incomplete, and would invite the follow-up question about when and how the pattern had been discovered, to which the honest answer involved a routing change nobody had escalated and a log retention policy that made attribution impossible.

What she kept returning to was Rhea's line about accounting choices. Somebody had decided, in a conference room in Chennai in September 2022, that a note was either acceptable or it was not, and that intensive-care cases would be left out because reviewer time was expensive. That decision had won a contract, defined a dashboard, shaped four years of engineering priorities, appeared in a proposal in New Jersey, and was about to be repeated in Dubai. Nobody had made it as a clinical decision. It had been made as a commercial one and then quietly promoted into the truth.

Outside, the last of the Sunday traffic thinned out along the Road No. 36 flyover. The steering committee was in seven hours and forty minutes. Ira had a page with three options on it and a sentence underneath them that she still did not know whether to say out loud.

Sujhav Systems: Forty Per Cent Better Than What?

Pune, September 2026. A cheaper, faster, higher-scoring model is available. Nobody at Sujhav can yet say whether it would make the product better.

1. The morning of 8 September

The Ganpati immersion processions had blocked Senapati Bapat Road for most of the previous evening, and half of Sujhav Systems' Pune office had worked from home. Ananya Deshpande, Head of Product, was in early anyway, because at 7.40 a.m. she had received a message from Vikram Sule, the founder and chief executive, that read: Customer advisory board is 26 September. I want to open with the new model. 40% better on the vendor's own tests and half the cost. Please confirm we are shipping.

Eighteen days. In that window Sujhav also had to close a renewal with its largest international customer, and India's festive retail peak — Navratri from 11 October, Diwali on 8 November — would begin loading the platform from the first week of October. Ananya's difficulty was not that she disagreed with Vikram. It was that she could not yet answer a simpler question: forty per cent better at what?

2. Sujhav Systems

Sujhav sells customer-support automation to consumer brands. Its product, Sujhav Reply, sits between a brand's helpdesk and its customers, reading incoming tickets — email, WhatsApp, the chat widget on the brand's site — and either answering them outright or drafting a reply for a human agent to approve. It handles order status, returns and exchanges, size and fit, warranty, and payment-failure queries, drawing on each brand's own policy documents, its order database, and the payment gateway's status feed.

The company was founded in 2021 by Vikram Sule and Rohan Iyer, both formerly at a Bengaluru enterprise-software company. Their thesis was that the D2C boom — the wave of Indian brands selling directly through their own storefronts and through Nykaa, Myntra, Flipkart and Amazon — had created hundreds of companies with the support volume of a large enterprise and the support team of a small one. Sujhav now serves 138 brands, mostly in apparel, beauty, small appliances and eyewear, and processes about 42 lakh tickets a month. Annual recurring revenue stands at ₹74 crore. The market it competes in is crowded: Freshworks and Zoho sell adjacent products to the same buyers, several well-funded startups sell the same promise, and the largest brands increasingly ask whether they should simply build on a model API themselves.

Roughly 61 per cent of Sujhav's tickets arrive in English, 27 per cent in Hinglish — Hindi written in Roman script, often mixed with English mid-sentence — and the remainder in Tamil, Marathi, Bengali and Telugu. About 18 per cent of revenue comes from outside India, almost all of it from the Gulf, where Sujhav's single largest customer is Al Zohour Retail, a Dubai-based fashion and beauty group whose contract, worth ₹1.9 crore a year, comes up for renewal on 30 September.

3. The situation

On 19 August, Sujhav's model vendor released a new model. Rohan Iyer, now Chief Technology Officer and based in Bengaluru, ran it through Sujhav's load harness within four days and circulated the results: median response latency down from 3.1 seconds to 1.4, cost per resolved ticket down from ₹0.61 to ₹0.29. The vendor's published evaluation suite showed the new model roughly forty per cent better on a composite of reasoning and instruction-following tests. At Sujhav's volume, the cost change alone was worth about ₹13.4 lakh a month, or ₹1.6 crore a year, against a hosting and inference line that the board had flagged twice.

Priyanka Nair, who runs customer success from Singapore and owns the Gulf accounts, replied to Rohan's note the same day. Al Zohour's support head had complained twice in July about replies to Arabic-script and mixed Arabic-English tickets being unnecessarily formal and occasionally wrong about exchange windows during Ramadan promotions. Priyanka wanted to know whether the new model was better or worse on exactly that. Nobody could tell her, because Sujhav had never measured it.

Naomi Chatterjee, a data scientist in Toronto who had joined in January, spent the last week of August building what she called, in her note to Ananya, "the smallest honest test we can run". She took 120 tickets sampled from July traffic, stratified so that the language mix matched production, and had two support-operations analysts in Pune grade both systems' outputs blind, against a criterion she wrote down before running anything: the reply must be consistent with the brand's own policy document, must not invent a policy, a fee or a date, and must not require the customer to write again to get an answer. All three conditions had to hold for a ticket to count as a pass.

Lucia Brandt, the design lead in Berlin, added a fourth concern that no one had scored. The new model wrote longer replies — noticeably longer — and about seventy per cent of Sujhav's end-customers read replies on a phone, often inside WhatsApp, where a long message is collapsed behind a "read more" link.

4. The people

Ananya Deshpande, Head of Product, Pune. Nine years in product, three at Sujhav. She wants a decision she can defend in December, when the festive numbers are read, and is uncomfortable that the only quantitative claim in circulation was produced by the party selling the model.

Vikram Sule, founder and CEO, Pune and often Mumbai. He is raising a Series C in the first quarter of 2027 and needs a visible story about margin and speed. He is not asking anyone to mislead a customer; he genuinely believes the vendor's number is informative and that Ananya is being slow.

Rohan Iyer, CTO, Bengaluru. He built the load harness and considers the engineering evidence complete: faster, cheaper, higher-scoring. He points out, fairly, that Sujhav has upgraded models three times before without incident.

Priyanka Nair, VP Customer Success, Singapore. She carries the Al Zohour relationship and remembers that the July complaints took six weeks to close. She wants no change to anything in the Gulf accounts before 30 September.

Naomi Chatterjee, data scientist, Toronto. She built the 120-ticket test and is careful about what it can and cannot support. Her working day overlaps Pune's by about two hours, which has slowed every exchange in this argument by a day.

Sameer Talwar, sales head, New Jersey. He has two North American pilots that were sold partly on response speed and would like the latency improvement announced immediately.

5. Exhibits

Read together, the exhibits say something Rohan's note did not. Exhibit 2's paired table shows a genuine improvement: of the 120 tickets, only 19 changed verdict at all, 14 in favour of the new model and 5 against. That is a real gain, and the direction is not in doubt. But the segment rows underneath show where it lives. English improves by nearly fourteen points. Hinglish improves modestly. Tamil, Marathi, Bengali and Telugu, grouped together in a sample of only sixteen tickets, appear to get worse — three tickets' worth, which is too few to be certain of anything and too many to ignore before a festive peak. And the segment Priyanka is most worried about was never sampled at all.

"We are not arguing about the model," Naomi wrote to Ananya on 6 September, at 11.40 p.m. Toronto time. "We are arguing about a sample of sixteen tickets and a segment of zero tickets. Both of those are fixable in nine days. Neither is fixable in a slide."

6. The options

Option A: ship to all customers before 26 September. Vikram gets his advisory-board opening, Sameer gets his latency story, and Sujhav banks ₹13.4 lakh a month, rising to roughly ₹27 lakh during the festive doubling. The cost is that the company would be making a full-population change on evidence covering 88 per cent of its language mix, with a visible regression signal in one segment and no data at all on its largest international account, three weeks before that account renews.

Option B: hold the change, extend the test to 350 tickets including Gulf coverage, and decide on 22 September. This costs ₹3.4 lakh and nine working days, requires hiring an Arabic-reading grader through Priyanka's Singapore team, and would give Ananya a properly stratified answer with each segment separately reported. It also means the advisory board hears a story about method rather than a headline, and forgoes about ₹9 lakh of saving in the interim.

Option C: ship to a limited slice now and measure in production. Route 15 per cent of English-language tickets, excluding all Gulf accounts and all non-Hinglish Indian languages, to the new model from 10 September, with escalation rate — the share of automated replies that a customer answers with a follow-up or that an agent reopens — as the guardrail, and an automatic revert if it rises by more than one point. This captures a smaller saving immediately, produces evidence from real customers rather than a sample, and leaves the risky segments untouched. The cost is complexity in routing, a partial answer, and a slower path to the full ₹13.4 lakh.

7. Questions for discussion

1. The vendor's suite and Naomi's 120 tickets both produced a number. What exactly is each one a measurement of, and why do they disagree about the size of the improvement?

2. Exhibit 2 shows fourteen tickets fixed and five broken. What would you want to know about those five before ship, and what would you do if all five came from a single large brand?

3. The "other Indian languages" row rests on sixteen tickets. Is that evidence of a regression, evidence of nothing, or evidence of a gap in the instrument? How should Ananya describe it to Vikram?

4. What should Ananya do by 26 September, and what precisely should she say to the customer advisory board and to Al Zohour?

8. A note for the learner

The lens for this case is the distinction between a benchmark and an eval. A benchmark is a score for a model on somebody else's fixed test. An eval is a repeatable measurement of your whole system on your task, against a criterion you stated before you looked at the results. The vendor's forty per cent is a benchmark. Naomi's 120 tickets, criterion written in advance, both systems answering the same inputs, blind human grading, is an eval — a small, incomplete, honest one. Almost all of the disagreement inside Sujhav dissolves once people notice they are citing two different kinds of evidence for two different objects.

A well-reasoned answer will do three things. It will treat the paired structure of Exhibit 2 as the important feature: because both systems answered the same 120 tickets, the meaningful quantities are the fourteen fixes and five breaks, not the difference of two percentages. It will refuse to average across segments that behave differently, and will notice that the segment share in the sample is not the same as the segment share in traffic. And it will state plainly that a claim about the Gulf accounts cannot be made from a sample containing no Gulf tickets, however good the rest of the evidence is.

One defensible path is a combination of B and C, sequenced so that nothing is lost. On 9 September Ananya commissions the 350-ticket stratified set, with Priyanka arranging an Arabic-reading grader in Singapore and Naomi writing the criterion and the shipping rule before any grading begins: ship if the paired improvement is positive on the whole set and no named segment regresses by more than two points. In parallel, from 10 September, she runs Option C's canary on English-language tickets only, excluding Gulf accounts entirely, with escalation rate as the guardrail. By 22 September she has both an offline answer with segment coverage and two weeks of live behavioural evidence on the safest segment. At the advisory board on 26 September she reports the canary result, which is real, customer-facing and hers rather than the vendor's. Al Zohour renews against an unchanged system, and the Gulf decision is taken in October on evidence that actually includes Arabic.

The reasoning is one of asymmetry. The upside of shipping three weeks early is roughly ₹9 lakh. The downside is a quality regression in Tamil and Bengali tickets during the highest-volume, lowest-tolerance weeks of the Indian retail year, and an unmeasured change to the system serving a ₹1.9 crore account in the fortnight before it signs. Spending ₹3.4 lakh and nine days to convert an untested claim into a measured one is cheap insurance. The point Ananya should make to Vikram is not that the new model is bad — the evidence suggests it is better — but that "forty per cent better" is a sentence about the vendor's test, and Sujhav's customers do not live inside it.

Evals and what they actually measure

A measurement is only as good as the population it samples, the criterion it encodes and the grader that applies it. Most arguments about model quality are really arguments about one of those three.

1. Two rooms, one week apart

On 11 March 2026, in a converted textile godown in Lower Parel that serves as Guftagu's Mumbai office, Sneha Kulkarni was looking at a slide she did not believe. Guftagu is a voice-first assistant for Indian-language users — 1.9 crore monthly actives, roughly two-thirds of them on entry-level Android handsets, asking for mandi prices, recipes, government-scheme eligibility, cricket scores and news read aloud in Marathi, Bhojpuri, Telugu and eight other languages. The slide reported that a rewritten answer-generation prompt had improved "helpfulness" from 66.8 to 75.2 on the team's 400-item evaluation set: an 8.4-point gain, graded by a judge model, achieved in nine days. Sneha, who had been VP Product for two years and a data scientist before that, asked the only question that mattered: if we are 8.4 points more helpful, why did the last three shipments that showed gains like this move no user behaviour at all?

Eight days later and 980 kilometres away, in Sanketa Insure Cloud's office off Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru, Devashish Menon faced a decision with a deadline attached. Sanketa sells claims-triage software to eleven Indian general insurers and two in the Gulf. Its system reads a motor claim — the first-notice-of-loss text, the surveyor's note, photographs, the policy record — and routes it: straight-through settlement, standard assessment, or referral to the special investigations unit. Sanketa's largest customer had asked, in a procurement review scheduled for 27 March, for evidence that a proposed model upgrade would not increase leakage. Devashish's team had a number ready: accuracy 95.6 per cent on a 500-claim test set, up from 94.9. He also had a nagging memory from a statistics course that a model which referred nothing at all would score 96.0 per cent on the same set.

Both people had a number. Neither number answered the question they were being asked. The distance between having a number and having an answer is the subject of this page.

2. The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree about it

An eval is a repeatable measurement of a system's behaviour on a fixed set of inputs, scored against a criterion stated in advance. The definition is unglamorous and every clause is load-bearing. It is repeatable, so that two runs separated by a quarter are comparable. It measures a system — the deployed assembly of retrieval, prompt, model, tools and post-processing — not a model in isolation. Its inputs are fixed, so that a difference in score is attributable to the change under test rather than to a change in the questions. It is scored, meaning a grader assigns verdicts. And its criterion is stated in advance, which is what distinguishes a decision procedure from an exercise in retrospective justification.

The lineage runs through information retrieval. Cyril Cleverdon's Cranfield experiments in the late 1950s and 1960s established the shape: a fixed document collection, a fixed set of queries, human relevance judgements, and a metric computed the same way for every system. The United States National Institute of Standards and Technology industrialised this as TREC from 1992. Machine learning adopted the same architecture with MNIST and, from 2009, ImageNet, whose frozen labelled test set became the referee for a decade of computer vision and, not coincidentally, the object of a decade of overfitting. Natural-language processing built GLUE in 2018, watched it saturate within a year, built SuperGLUE, watched that saturate too, and by 2022 was reaching for broader instruments such as Stanford's HELM, which reported many metrics across many scenarios precisely because a single headline number had stopped being informative.

The problem all of this was invented to solve is that a demonstration proves nothing about a probabilistic function. A language model samples from a distribution over next tokens; the same prompt run twice can produce two different answers, one excellent and one wrong. A screenshot is a sample of size one. An eval converts anecdote into an estimate with a known, or at least knowable, error.

Within that shared definition, three schools genuinely disagree, and a product manager who cannot tell them apart will mediate their arguments badly.

The measurement school treats evals as psychometrics. Its central commitment is that a score means nothing without construct validity: you must be able to say what latent quality the score is a measure of, show that the items sample that construct, and report reliability. Adherents will sign the proposition that an eval whose grader's inter-rater agreement has never been measured is not a measurement. They will not sign the proposition that a fast, rough eval is better than none; they think a badly validated number is worse than no number, because it commands the authority of arithmetic without the substance.

The engineering school treats evals as regression tests. Its commitment is that the point of an eval is to catch breakage in continuous integration, cheaply and often. It will sign a 60-item eval that runs on every pull request is worth more than a 2,000-item eval that runs quarterly. It will not sign the psychometricians' insistence on validation before use; it argues, with evidence, that most real damage comes from obvious regressions that any crude test catches, and that validation rigour is a tax that stops teams from testing at all.

The product school treats evals as proxies whose only justification is their correlation with a business outcome. It will sign an offline eval that has never been checked against a live experiment is a hypothesis, not evidence. It will not sign that offline evals can stand alone; where volume permits an online test, it regards the offline number as a screening device and nothing more. Sneha at Guftagu is, by temperament, in this school. Devashish at Sanketa cannot be, because he serves eleven insurers and cannot run a randomised experiment on fraud referral without a regulator asking why.

The three schools are not reconcilable by synthesis. They optimise for different error costs: the measurement school fears believing a false number, the engineering school fears shipping an unnoticed break, the product school fears improving a metric nobody's business depends on. Which fear is correct depends on the product.

3. Mechanics in depth

An expert building an eval works through seven decisions. The first three are usually discussed; the last four are usually implicit, and are where the failures live.

The unit. What is one observation? For Sanketa it is one claim passing through the full pipeline, including the optical character recognition on the surveyor's note, which fails on roughly four per cent of handwritten Hindi forms and produces a downstream error the model is then blamed for. Choosing the model output as the unit would exclude the OCR stage and would systematically flatter every model comparison.

The population and the sample. A fixed set is a sample from a population, and the population is whatever traffic the system will see next quarter, not last. Sanketa's 500-claim set was drawn in July 2025 from four insurers. By March 2026 two more insurers had joined, one of them writing predominantly commercial-vehicle policies in Gujarat with a very different claim profile. The set was no longer a sample of the population; it was a sample of a population that had ceased to exist. Stratifying — drawing a fixed proportion from each named segment and re-weighting to the current traffic mix at scoring time — is the standard repair, and it is skipped constantly.

The criterion. This is a product judgement wearing technical clothing. Sanketa's original criterion was "correct routing decision", which treats a missed fraud referral and an unnecessary referral as equally bad. They are not remotely equal, as the arithmetic below shows. Guftagu's criterion was "helpfulness", which is not a criterion at all but a placeholder for one; when Sneha asked her team to write down what a judge should look for, four engineers produced four different rubrics.

The grader and its error. Graders make mistakes, and grader error attenuates every difference the eval reports. Suppose the true state of an item is pass or fail, and the grader independently flips the verdict with probability e. Then an observed pass rate is a mixture, and the observed difference between two systems shrinks toward zero by a factor of (1 − 2e). At e = 0.12 — a plausible error rate for a competent judge model on a subjective rubric — a true five-point gap reads as 5 × 0.76 = 3.8 points. The direction is preserved; the magnitude is not. Teams that compare a measured gap against a fixed shipping threshold, without accounting for attenuation, systematically under-ship real improvements and over-trust small ones.

Grader agreement is quantified with Cohen's kappa, which corrects raw agreement for agreement expected by chance. On Sanketa's 40-claim calibration exercise, two senior assessors — one in Bengaluru, one in Pune — graded blind. Assessor A passed 30 items, Assessor B passed 28, and they agreed on 34. Raw agreement is 34/40 = 0.85. Expected agreement is (30/40 × 28/40) + (10/40 × 12/40) = 0.525 + 0.075 = 0.60. Kappa is (0.85 − 0.60)/(1 − 0.60) = 0.25/0.40 = 0.625. That is substantial by convention and mediocre in practice: it means the instrument cannot reliably resolve differences of the same order as its own noise.

Repetition. Generation is sampled. One run per item measures a draw, not a system. Running k times per item and reporting the proportion of runs that pass gives an estimate of per-item reliability, which is often the thing users actually feel — an assistant that is right four times in five is experienced very differently from one that is right every time on a smaller set of questions.

The statistical design and how big the set must be. Because the same items are given to both systems, the correct test is paired. McNemar's statistic uses only the discordant items: z = (b − c) / √(b + c), where b is the count the challenger fixes and c the count it breaks. This lets you size the set before running it. Suppose you expect 12 per cent of items to change verdict, three fixes for every break: then b = 0.09n, c = 0.03n, and z = 0.06n / √(0.12n) = 0.173√n. To reach the conventional 1.96 you need √n = 11.3, so n = 128 items. To reach 2.80, which buys roughly 80 per cent power rather than a coin-flip chance of detection, you need √n = 16.2, so n = 262. That single line of algebra answers the question every team asks and almost none computes: how many items is enough.

The decision rule. Written before the run: the threshold, the protected segments that may not regress, and what happens if the result is ambiguous. An eval without a pre-registered decision rule reliably produces the decision its owner already preferred.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

The conditions can be written as testable claims, which is more useful than a list of caveats.

Claim one: the task has a criterion two competent people would agree on after discussion. For Sanketa this holds — whether a claim warranted investigation is settled by what the investigation found. For Guftagu it partly fails: whether a two-sentence Marathi answer about a scheme deadline was "helpful" depends on a user's literacy, their handset, whether they were driving, and what they would have done otherwise. Where the criterion is contested, an eval still has value, but only as a comparison instrument — it can say A beats B under this rubric; it cannot say A is good.

Claim two: the fixed set is a current sample of the population you will serve. Sanketa fails this outright; the set predates two customers. Guftagu passes on volume and fails on language coverage: 71 per cent of its 400 items are Hindi, against 44 per cent of production traffic, because the eval was assembled by the Delhi content team.

Claim three: the difference you care about is larger than the noise floor set by grader error and sampling. With kappa at 0.625 and 500 items, Sanketa can resolve a difference of a few points, not a difference of half a point. Devashish's 0.7-point accuracy gain is inside the noise and would be inside it even if accuracy were the right metric.

Claim four: nothing downstream reacts to the measurement in a way that invalidates it. This is the Goodhart condition, and it fails progressively rather than suddenly. An eval used weekly by engineers who can see the items becomes, over months, a specification the system is fitted to.

The idea is actively misleading in two situations. The first is rare, high-severity events. If a catastrophic failure occurs in one interaction in 5,000, a 500-item eval will observe zero of them nearly always; the rule of three says that observing zero events in n trials is consistent with a true rate as high as 3/n, so zero in 500 is consistent with one in 167. Reporting "no safety failures in the eval" from such a set is not evidence of safety; it is evidence that the instrument cannot see the thing being asked about. The second is products where the value is in the tail of user intent — open-ended assistants, search, creative tools — where any fixed set of a few hundred items samples the head and tells you nothing about the long tail that generates the complaints.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product companies. When one shared model serves four products, the eval question becomes political rather than technical. Sanketa's model serves motor, health and marine claims. A model change that improves motor by four points and degrades marine by three is a net gain if you weight by volume and a net loss if you weight by revenue, because marine claims are twenty times larger. Mature companies resolve this with per-product gates rather than a portfolio average, and pay for it in shipping velocity: any product can block. Less mature companies compute the average and discover the disagreement in a customer escalation.

Two-sided products. A marketplace assistant serves buyers and sellers, whose criteria conflict on the same output. A refund answer that is generous to the buyer is expensive to the seller. A single pass rate silently averages two objectives and hides the trade-off; the honest design maintains two evals with two rubrics and reports both, accepting that some changes will be improvements on one side only.

Regulated products. Under the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority's expectations for claims handling, and increasingly under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act for the data used, Sanketa's evidence has to survive an audit. That changes the eval from an internal instrument into a document: the set must be retained, the grading provenance recorded, the criterion dated. It also creates a perverse pressure — anything measured must be disclosed, so there is a quiet incentive not to measure the segments where you suspect you are weak. Devashish has heard this argued in a meeting and did not enjoy it.

Hardware plus software. Guftagu runs on handsets ranging from a ₹6,500 entry-level phone to a ₹90,000 flagship. On the cheap handset, a model that generates 40 per cent more tokens raises perceived latency past the point where users interrupt the answer. An eval run on server infrastructure measures a system no user has. The repair is to include device class as a stratum and measure time-to-first-useful-word, not answer quality alone.

AI-native organisational seams. The deepest problem is ownership. At Guftagu the eval set belongs to the applied-science team in Bengaluru, the rubric to the content team in Delhi, the judge prompt to a contractor, and the shipping decision to Sneha in Mumbai. Nobody owns the question "is this set still representative", so nobody asks it. Mature companies solve this by naming a single owner for the instrument, separate from the owner of the system being measured — the same separation an audit function has from the business it audits — and by rotating a fresh held-out sample that the engineers optimising the system never see.

6. Nuances that separate the expert from the competent

The word "eval" hides a category error

A benchmark measures a model on someone's public task; an eval measures your system on your task. The tell is when a shipping argument cites a number nobody in the room can attach an input to. An expert's first move is not to dispute the number but to ask to see ten items from the set. The obvious reading — that a better model must make a better product — is wrong because five of the six components in a typical pipeline are unchanged, and some of them were tuned to the old model's quirks.

Accuracy is almost always the wrong metric under class imbalance

Devashish's memory was correct. On his 500-claim set with 20 true referrals, a system that refers nothing scores 96.0 per cent accuracy. The tell an expert looks for is a metric whose value is close to the base rate of the majority class. The right instruments are precision and recall, and, better, an explicit cost function — which requires the business to state what a miss costs, a conversation many teams avoid because the answer is embarrassing.

Grader error attenuates, it does not merely add noise

Most people treat a noisy grader as something that widens confidence intervals. It also biases the estimated effect size toward zero by the factor (1 − 2e). The tell is a team whose evals consistently show small positive effects that fail to reproduce in the field at the magnitude claimed, and who conclude their eval is too conservative. It is; and the fix is to measure e against a human-labelled subset, not to lower the threshold.

A judge model inherits the biases of a model

Judge models prefer longer answers, prefer answers formatted like their own, and prefer confident phrasing over hedged phrasing even when hedging is correct. The tell is a change that improves the eval score while increasing mean answer length — a correlation worth plotting on every run. Guftagu's 8.4-point gain came with a 34 per cent increase in mean answer length, which on an entry-level handset is a regression, not an improvement.

Offline gains and online gains are different quantities, related by an unknown function

An offline eval measures output quality under a rubric. An online experiment measures behaviour. The relationship between them is empirical and product-specific, and most teams never estimate it. The expert's move is to keep a log: for every shipped change, the offline delta and the subsequent online delta. After a dozen entries you know your conversion rate, and you know whether your eval is predictive or decorative.

A frozen set becomes a specification

The moment engineers can inspect the items, optimisation against them begins, honestly and unconsciously. The tell is a pass rate that rises steadily over months while support tickets do not fall. The counter-measure is a rotating held-out sample, drawn from live traffic, graded once, never shown to the team, and used only to check that the visible set still predicts the invisible one.

Aggregates can reverse under stratification

When segments differ in both difficulty and volume, an overall improvement can coexist with a decline in the segment carrying most of the traffic. The tell is a report with one number and no segment table. Experts insist on protected segments named before the run, and on a paired contingency table showing fixes and breaks, because "how many things got worse" is a question an average is structurally unable to answer.

Per-item reliability differs from per-set pass rate

Two systems can pass 78 per cent of items and feel entirely different: one passes 78 per cent of items every time, the other passes every item 78 per cent of the time. Users experience the second as unreliable and the first as limited, and the product responses differ — the first needs coverage, the second needs constraint. The tell is a team that runs each item once and therefore cannot distinguish the two.

Zero observed failures is not a rate of zero

The rule of three — the 95 per cent upper bound on a rate when zero events are observed in n trials is approximately 3/n — is the single most useful piece of arithmetic for reading safety claims. Zero in 200 means "possibly as bad as one in 67". Experts state the bound rather than the count.

The cost of the eval belongs in the decision

A 2,000-item human-graded set at eight minutes per item is 267 hours, roughly ₹4.8 lakh at Indian analyst rates and considerably more at Toronto or Berlin rates. That is worth paying against a decision worth crores and absurd against a decision worth lakhs. The expert sizes the instrument to the decision, and says out loud when the honest answer is "we will ship this on judgement because measuring it costs more than being wrong".

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products with large volume, the offline eval is a screen and the online experiment is the referee. Guftagu can randomise 4 per cent of 1.9 crore users and detect small behavioural effects; its offline set exists to prevent obviously bad candidates from reaching that experiment and to catch safety regressions that must never be tested on users at all.

In enterprise B2B, the offline eval is the referee, because there is no experiment to run: eleven insurers, contractual obligations, and a regulator make randomisation on claims outcomes impossible. The eval is also an external artefact, produced in procurement reviews and audits, which changes its design — provenance and reproducibility matter more than speed.

In platforms and marketplaces the distinguishing feature is conflicting criteria across sides, discussed above. In hardware-plus-software the distinguishing feature is that the deployment environment is part of the system, so device strata belong in the set. In AI-native products the distinguishing feature is that the model is a supplier who changes the product without telling you, which makes continuous re-running of the same set the primary control rather than an occasional exercise.

Stage changes what is affordable, not what is true. A ten-person company should run 60 items graded by a founder, monthly; the founder's grading is high-quality because criterion and judgement sit in one head, and the honest limitation is that 60 items cannot detect anything smaller than a large effect. A company of Sanketa's size — 240 people, ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue — can afford stratified sets, calibrated grader panels and continuous runs, and will lose instead to organisational drift: the set becomes an owned asset, refreshing it becomes a quarterly project, and the criterion slowly detaches from any living user.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Benchmark substitution. Early sign: a shipping deck citing a vendor score. Diagnostic question: show me ten inputs from that set. Cost of catching it late: an upgrade that degrades the segments the public benchmark does not cover, discovered by a customer.

Criterion drift. Early sign: the metric named in the review differs from the metric in last quarter's review, with no written change. Diagnostic: ask for the dated criterion document. Cost of catching it late: a year of incomparable numbers and a team that cannot say whether the product improved.

Silent overfitting. Early sign: pass rate rising while complaints hold flat. Diagnostic: run a fresh sample this week. Cost: as at Guftagu, a quarter to rebuild and a credibility loss that outlasts it.

Underpowered decisions. Early sign: decisions taken on differences of two or three points on sets of a hundred. Diagnostic: how many items changed verdict? Cost: a random walk in which every second shipment quietly undoes the previous one.

Instrument capture. Early sign: the team that builds the system also owns the set, the rubric and the report. Diagnostic: who can veto a shipment on the evidence? Cost: the eval becomes a ceremony, and its numbers become unusable in exactly the audit or procurement review they were built for.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should LLM-as-judge be trusted for shipping decisions? The case for: judges validated against human labels reach kappa in the 0.6 to 0.8 range on well-specified rubrics, cost a hundredth of human grading, and allow sets large enough to be powered. If you demand human grading you will run 80 items instead of 2,000 and your instrument will be blind. For this to be wrong, judge biases would have to correlate with the changes teams actually make — which, on length, they demonstrably do. The case against: a judge is a model, so it shares failure modes with the system it grades, and a shared blind spot produces confident agreement rather than detected error. For this to be wrong, judges from a different model family would have to show independent errors, which is partly but not wholly supported.

Should offline evals gate shipping at all in high-volume consumer products? The case for gating: users are not a test population, and some regressions are unacceptable at any sample size. The case against: offline rubrics measure what raters like, live experiments measure what users do, and where the two conflict the users are right; gating on the rubric systematically ships the preferences of a small content team to a hundred million people. What would settle it is a company-specific correlation log, which almost nobody keeps.

Should the eval set be visible to the engineers optimising against it? The engineering school says yes: you cannot debug what you cannot read, and the alternative is slow, blind iteration. The measurement school says no: visibility converts the instrument into a target and destroys it, as at Guftagu. The practical settlement — visible regression set plus hidden measurement set — is widely recommended and unevenly practised, because maintaining two instruments costs twice as much and only one of them makes anyone's dashboard go up.

Is there such a thing as a general-purpose quality eval? Vendors sell them; several serious practitioners argue that a well-constructed general rubric transfers across tasks better than each team's homemade set. The opposing position holds that quality is defined by the job to be done, so a general eval measures a construct no user has. The evidence is mixed and, tellingly, mostly published by parties with an interest.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied evals asks for the number. Someone who has internalised them asks four questions in a specific order: what population is this a sample of, who wrote the criterion and when, what is the grader's error, and how many items changed verdict. They size the instrument to the decision rather than to convention, and say so when the honest answer is that measuring costs more than being wrong. They keep a log relating offline deltas to online outcomes, because they know their eval's predictive value is an empirical fact about their product and not a property of evals in general. They separate the instrument's owner from the system's owner. They report bounds rather than counts for rare events. And when a colleague presents a two-point improvement, their instinct is neither belief nor scepticism but a question about the discordant cells.

Sneha rejected the prompt shipment and reorganised the instrument instead. Her reasoning was that an 8.4-point gain accompanied by a 34 per cent length increase and a seven-point rise in interruptions on low-RAM handsets is a measurement of the judge's preferences, not the users'; and that until the hidden set existed, no future number would be worth arguing about either. She accepted a quarter of visible stagnation to buy an instrument she could believe.

Devashish did not have that luxury; the procurement review was on 27 March. His judgement was that a customer shown an honest weakness alongside a defensible cost argument is easier to keep than a customer shown a flattering number that a later audit contradicts.

1. Sanketa's accuracy figure and its cost-weighted figure rank the same two systems in opposite orders. Who in the company should own the choice of criterion, and what does your answer imply about where the eval function should report?

2. Guftagu's visible set rose eighteen points above its hidden set over nine months. At what point in that nine months could the divergence have been detected cheaply, and what would have had to be true about the organisation for anyone to have looked?

3. Suppose a judge model has an error rate of 12 per cent and a human panel costs twenty times as much. Under what conditions is the cheap instrument the right choice, and how would you state that condition to a board in one sentence?

13. Going deeper

What a large language model actually is matters next because the whole justification for measuring rather than demonstrating rests on the model being a sampled probabilistic function; understanding that makes repetition and variance intuitive rather than pedantic. Hallucination and confabulation supplies the specific failure modes an eval's criterion has to encode, and explains why "factually consistent with the retrieved document" is a sharper clause than "correct". Problem–model fit is the discipline that decides whether the task is worth measuring at all, which is the one question an eval structurally cannot answer.

Golden sets and LLM-as-judge is the direct sequel: it unlocks the ability to run sets large enough to be powered, and teaches the validation step without which a judge's verdicts are decoration. Benchmarks, leaderboards and what SOTA means sharpens the component-versus-system distinction that this page rests on, and inoculates against the most common shipping error. Drift and silent regression covers the case where nothing in your system changed but your supplier's model did, which is the dominant risk in AI-native products. Model cards and documentation is how the results become an external artefact that survives a procurement review or an audit.

Further down, tokens and tokenisation and the context window explain why Indian-language performance and cost behave the way they do — Devanagari and Telugu consume substantially more tokens per unit of meaning than English, which is quietly why Guftagu's per-session cost varies by language. The transformer and attention, embeddings and vector search and similarity explain the retrieval stage whose quality your eval is silently measuring alongside the model. Inference versus training clarifies which of your options are actually available: most product teams are choosing among prompts, retrieval and models at inference time, and an eval is the instrument that makes that choice a decision rather than a preference.
